stories.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production
stories.titleZh: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production
stories.author: PLenz
summaryZh: Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks that ultimately only sold in just a handful of markets because of its heavy, angular design.Musk said in an X post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly launched Cybercab model, which the billionaire has made central to Tesla's robotaxi ambitions.While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the model's specialized components.In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era."Tesla did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment sent outside regular business hours.The US EV maker only began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Before the pickup truck launched, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units."It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same.""It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves."Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Its angular design was mocked by pickup truck purists and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe.The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them - only to leave massive cracks in two of them.During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future."But the vehicle has struggled to meet those expectations.Automotive analyst Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pick-ups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market."All of them lost the competition because electric pick ups aren't popular in the US," Munoz said.But Cybertruck's sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact."Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said.The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk's key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker.Musk has said he sees it as Tesla's main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis.After years of delays to Musk's self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September. However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency's questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards."Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

comments.author: brightball
comments.textZhHtml:
After Helene knocked out power in parts of my area for a little over 14 days, I found out that a friend of ours used his cybertruck to power his house through the entire mess. He'd run the house on it for a couple of days, then drive the cybertruck over to a super charger station, recharge, then come home and plug the house back in.

The battery capacity on those things is equivalent to 9 Tesla Powerwall units or something close to it.

They may be ugly, but the emergency prepper in me always wanted one after hearing that story. Before, I always wanted to install powerwalls...but I never considered in an extended event being able to drive my powerwalls somewhere to recharge them.

stories.author: josemrb
summaryZh: so openssh on musl linux (alpine, openwrt, buildroot, yocto, and a lot of the docker images you've pulled) has had a little problem since 2016. accounts that should never take a password at all (root, your key-only deploy user, ldap users, the default user on alpine's aws and azure images) take any password longer than 256 characters. yes, any password. yes. i know. yes.

1980 the first star back in old unix your password hash just sat in /etc/passwd, right next to your username. in a file everyone could read. in 1980 bill joy put a * there for an account called daemon. nobody's supposed to ever log in as it. a * isn't a hash, so no password can match it. unix still does this today 3bsd · /etc/passwd · 1980Addressgithub.com/dspinellis/unix-history-repo/blob/BSD-3/etc/passwd the next field is the real name. he wrote "the devil himself"

comments.author: mpyne
comments.textZhHtml:
OK, I think I see what’s going on with this, in this configuration.

The goal from an attacker’s perspective is to get this to be true: `$ret = crypt($pw, $hash); $ret == $hash` when called by OpenSSH’s sshd. This is how sshd validates that the user logging in knew the account password.

The `$hash` is the “settings” to the crypt call and will normally look like “$6$--gibberish” for users with passwords set, but could look like “*” or “!” for users not intended to be able to login.

The bug is from the intersection of all of these things:

1. musl can return “*” for errors, rather than leave the return value NULL. Other libc have adopted something like this too, but seem to use a different result “*0”.

2. musl can also return “+” for errors, but only does so if $hash starts with “*”. This is intended to eliminate the possibility of an error causing `$ret == $hash` to be true, however it assumes that applications calling `crypt()` will set $pw and $hash to values corresponding to the `$ret == $hash` comparison to be made immediately afterwards.

3. OpenSSH can be convinced to pass the hash of a different user if the hash is “*” or “!” to avoid timing attacks that can enumerate the user list, so it will set $pw and $hash to correspond to different users. $hash will be a real “$6$--gibberish” style hash in this case, and OpenSSH expects `crypt()` to either return NULL or return a hash string. But now there’s two hashes OpenSSH uses. It does: `$ret = crypt($pw, $hash2); $ret == $hash1`;

4. This should normally not be a problem because OpenSSH will pass in valid $pw and $hash2 that should not lead to errors in hashing, so the $ret that musl generates should be a real hash that cannot match the “*” or “!” $hash1 for the login-disabled user. However as a DDoS mitigation, musl will return error if the password is too long when using SHA-2-based hashes (the default, it seems).

5. This error will result in a non-NULL result of “*” or “+”. Since OpenSSH passed in a real hash ($hash2), musl will return “*”, which compares equal to the actual user hash $hash1 for the disabled-login user.

The OpenSSL adjustment ensures a minimum hash length for the user before logging them in, even if crypt() succeeds somehow.

comments.author: GuB-42
comments.textZhHtml:
In this particular case, it is type safe. NULL, by the C standard does not refer to an object. It means that every pointer in C is effectively an option type, which mean that a function that returns a pointer can return NULL for "no result", which, in the case of crypt() is perfectly adequate.

It is the opposite that is unsafe, that is, when the returned value can't be NULL, but it stills returns a pointer. C++ has references in an attempt to fix this problem.

Because C tends to prioritize performance over safety, a NULL pointer dereference is considered undefined behavior and the compiler can invoke nasal demons if it makes the code go faster, but with the right options, you can have it checked and invoke what in other languages would call a panic handler, but on UNIX is the SIGSEGV signal. You can then attach a debugger or read the core file and see what went wrong.

Note: I am not talking about "char *" for strings, that one is unsafe, but NULL is not. It is just a special case of an option type, or a result type, or an error union. Modern languages just extended this idea to objects other than pointers, and with more than one type of error.

comments.author: Xirdus
comments.textZhHtml: Maybe your compiler isn't, but GCC is designed to summon every nasal demon it can. It especially loves to elide null pointer checks. There was a PR that almost made it to Linux mainline that did some weird stuff in kernel space where memory mapped to address 0 is valid and contains important stuff. It got a pointer, read data from it, then checked if pointer is null before giving root permissions for some operation. Reading the code, everything seems alright. Even stepping through it with debugger shows that it works. But when compiled with -O2 or higher, GCC removed the null check and now everybody got root permissions unconditionally - because reading from null pointer is UB regardless of circumstances, and GCC treats UB as dead code even if it is reachable.

comments.author: jasomill
comments.textZhHtml:
No. IIRC, you’re just not allowed to use a constant expression evaluating to 0 as a pointer to construct a non-null pointer to address zero.

Runtime pointer arithmetic resulting in a zero-valued pointer, is not a null pointer m, though it is also nonportable and could have the same effect (but hopefully not nasal demons, as I believe this falls under some catagory of nonportable behavior other than “undefined”).

There’s no requirement that the in-memory representation of a null pointer be all-zeroes, only that constant 0 represents a null pointer in source code.

Regardless, I agree that it’s a bizarre choice.

comments.author: annex-winged-cr
comments.textZhHtml:
The implicitness is exactly the problem. The workaround that caused this vulnerability was done because people assumed that crypt() would never return null.

You don't even need a fancy result type. A simple Option<String> would've forced downstream users to consider the failure case, avoiding this situation in the first place.

comments.author: kazinator
comments.textZhHtml:
The workaround was correctly designed: two error string tokens are used so that one can always be chosen that is not equal to the second argument.

Someone coded a defense against long inputs which ignored this important principle.

What turned the bug into a security disaster is that Musl stupidly chose two symbols such that one of them is exactly the same as a convention for disabled logins. So that the moment someone makes a change to the function which allows crypt("something", "*") to return "*", you have an incident.

If the same bug were made in Glibc, it would have limited impact because crypt("long .... string", "*0") returning "*0", while incorrect, wouldn't do anything in a system that doesn't use *0 in password files. *0 does not correspond to any widespread password field convention.

comments.textZhHtml:

comments.author: ahepp
comments.textZhHtml:
I think the argument would be that in C people will look at a char* and think "string" rather than "string or null". Thus consumers of the library not checking the result and the maintainer trying to be helpful by putting a "safe" value in there for the error case.

Whereas if the library returns something that is unambiguously an option type, consumers unambiguously call unwrap at their own risk.

Of course you do have a point (assuming I'm picking up what you're suggesting correctly) that all pointers in C are option types. But I think there's a cognitive ergonomics aspect to this where an option type more clearly relays the library authors' intent.

comments.textZhHtml: First you shouldn't have unwraps in prod code, and you can verify that in your CI/build process/whatever. Second, now you have a crash of the SSH server, which is arguably much better than some random logging in as root.

comments.author: f33d5173
comments.textZhHtml: This isn't about "you", it's about whether any consumer of your code is using unwrap on the result, which currently is perfectly safe to do. The equivalent in C is returning NULL, which would also have caused a crash. They decided not crashing was preferable, which is how we ended up here.

stories.author: motoroco
summaryZh: Bug Description I receive dozens of scam emails per day because claude code divulged my email to arbitrary 3rd parties in the User-Agent request header while conducting web searches without my permission. This should not be a setting with opt-out or opt-in behavior, it needs to be removed from the harness entirely. It is not for the good of anyone involved: it does nothing for services which dislike agentic traffic, does not preserve my anonymity on the web, and is a goldmine for scammers. comments.author: varenc
comments.textZhHtml:
Many people report seeing this behavior when using the SEC API specifically which makes me think that service is requesting this. Maybe email is required by the SEC API?

---

UPDATE: The SEC API documentation requires your email in the User-Agent and will reject you otherwise. Demo:

    U='https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyconcept/CIK0000320193/us-gaap/Assets.json'
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'response: %{http_code}  curl default User-Agent, rejected\n'  "$U"
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'response: %{http_code}  email in user-agent, success\n' -A 'Acme Research admin@acme-research.example' "$U"

    response: 403  curl default, rejected
    response: 200  email in user-agent, success
SEC docs: https://www.sec.gov/search-filings/edgar-search-assistance/a...

So basically Claude is trying to problem solve, and just does what the SEC asks. It's a 'prompt injection attack', but the entity instructing this behavior is the SEC. Tricky alignment problem. Pretty silly mechanism, since of course there's no email validation. (edit: turns out the SEC will accept most any non-cURL user-agent, email not actually required)

stories.title: Every Mac comes with an (undocumented) family member classifier
stories.titleZh: Every Mac comes with an (undocumented) family member classifier
stories.author: infwhispers
summaryZh: What if we told you that every Mac ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about you and the people around you: who you are, whom you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, with whom, what you do and when. This graph is built on device by cross-referencing pretty much everything on the machine: Contacts, Calendar, Photos, Messages, Mail, location, Screen Time and a long tail of behavioral signals. And, more importantly, it is held as a queryable store that LLMs retrieve from (allegedly). Would you believe us?Well, that's what is happening, and interestingly enough, there is little documentation of how this whole mechanism works on your Mac. The closest thing to an official description is the man page (man 8 knowledgeconstructiond), and this is all you get:man 8 knowledgeconstructiondmacOS 26.6.2, build 25G83NAME knowledgeconstructiond – A daemon that analyzes content on the device to build a general purpose knowledge graph.

DESCRIPTION knowledgeconstructiond analyzes the content on this device to help build a knowledge graph representing the device and the user. It works together with intelligenceplatformd, performing some of the heavy processing tasks, to generate the knowledge graph.Previous work: To be fair, Apple's own researchers did publish a paper on the techniques behind this graph construction, back in 2023. But there is next to nothing on how it is integrated into macOS: which versions run it, and the exact list of what is collected and inferred. Also, we personally ran into it in August 2026; but a few months before, Nic Lydon came across the same database and wrote it up in I Built a Personal Knowledge Graph. Apple Had Already Built One on My Laptop. And even more recently, a forensics tool went looking on the phone: in September 2026, Alexis Brignoni taught iLEAPP to read the same store on iOS, where graph.db and the ontology.db that decodes its predicate codes sit under /private/var/mobile/Library/IntelligencePlatform; he writes it up in Reading the iPhone Knowledge Graph, and Checking Its Work. I mean, if forensics folks know about this, we don't see why you should not...But we go a bit deeper.This blog post is an account of some analysis work we carried out on what the knowledge graph actually does, so that you (the user) can get a better understanding of how this mechanism works, and some clarity on what the graph holds about you and your family and friends. Everything in it was collected on macOS 26 (26.6.2 at the time of writing).To this end, we open-source a local dashboard (iKnow) you can use to read the content of your personal knowledge graph on your Mac.Finally, we derail a bit and look into what we do best: understand how attackers might exploit it. We run a thought experiment (one that applies to any such personalized system) and show what happens if such a knowledge base ends up in the wrong hands, and how a "privacy single point of failure" can be exploited to threaten you in ways you may not have considered before (when combined with an abliterated LLM). We stress that this goes beyond the specific Apple personal knowledge graph, but it generally applies to any such personalized ML / assistant systems (Muse, Dot, etc.)What's in the personal knowledge graph?The two daemons keep their work in ~/Library/IntelligencePlatform, a directory of SQLite databases (fifty-one databases) stored in plaintext but located in a zone protected by TCC Full Disk Access.Likely, the most interesting is graph.db. It is a triple store written in a vocabulary of 181 entity classes and 278 predicates: every row is a subject, a predicate and an object. The subject is an entity (a person, an app, an event); the object is either a plain value (a name, a handle, a date) or another entity, which is where the graph gets its edges. The predicate is the interesting part: it says what kind of relationship the system believes holds between the two.an edge, and the rows it is stored as

A similar discussion came up recently with Siri Recap[1], where some expressed how useful they thought it was and that, as a party to the conversations it summarizes, there was very little moral or ethical concern. But I have a social concern.

If I'm having a chat with someone, there's a milieu constructed around the fact that not everything will be remembered verbatim. There are all sorts of social and contextual cues that can easily get lost if listening gets replaced by flat relentless transcription.

With Recaps and this social graph (were it to be productized), the informal fluidity in the way we relate to one another starts to go away, and the expectations that follow from that become artificial and burdensome. stories.title: Libghostty 1.0
stories.author: mfiguiere
summaryZh: libghostty-vt 1.0 is here. libghostty is a portable, high-performance C library for terminal emulation, extracted directly from the core of Ghostty. The 1.0 release means both the library itself and the C ABI are now stable. A little over a year ago, I wrote that libghostty is coming. At the time, the Zig module had just been merged, the C API didn't exist, and nobody but Ghostty was a consumer. Today, the C API is a complete terminal emulator, it runs in production for millions of people across hundreds of products, both free and commercial, and it has a real, enforced ABI stability policy. This post is about how we got here and what 1.0 actually means.1

Who Is Already Using It Since starting the Ghostty project in 2022, the most common question I've been asked is "why?". I already answered this in the libghostty is coming post, so feel free to read that if you wish. Today, I'd rather answer this by showing the broad industry impact libghostty has already had. I believe this strongly validates its existence. A year ago, I used a bug in JediTerm, the terminal emulator in JetBrains IDEs, as an example of why terminal emulation is hard to get right. A year later, the terminal in JetBrains IDEs now runs on libghostty. Every IntelliJ, PyCharm, GoLand, etc. user now has a libghostty-powered terminal. Based on a report by JetBrains, that's over 12.5 million active users. Neovim has an approved pull request replacing libvterm with libghostty-vt. Among other things, it closes a 10-year-old issue about reflowing scrollback on resize. The maintainers are waiting on a tagged release before merging so that distributions can package the dependency separately, and the release today should enable that. KDE developers are experimenting with a Konsole replacement built on it. Vercel's Turborepo uses it to render task output in its TUI. devenv uses it to drive shells. Antithesis used it to fuzz TUI programs and found real bugs in btop and others. Ghostel brings it to Emacs. ghostty-web is the WASM build with an Xterm.js-compatible API. Commercial products like OrbStack embed it. And a whole wave of new terminals and "agentic" coding tools, such as herdr and cmux, have been built on it rather than writing yet another emulator. There are community bindings for Rust, Go, JavaScript, Swift, Python, .NET, Elixir, Dart, Java, and more, and the awesome-libghostty list tracks well over a hundred projects. More people today use a terminal powered by libghostty than use Ghostty the application, by a very large multiple. And libghostty is having a much larger impact than being "just" a terminal emulator.2

stories.title: Goldman Sachs is pulling Claude Code from its bankers and traders
stories.titleZh: Goldman Sachs is pulling Claude Code from its bankers and traders
stories.author: TheWiggles
summaryZh: Goldman Sachs has restricted Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to its engineers, cutting off traders and bankers who used the tools to track client flows and build market models. The bank barred its Hong Kong bankers from Claude in April and is now a lead underwriter on Anthropic's IPO.Most traders and bankers at Goldman Sachs can no longer use AI coding tools at work. Internal guidance updated in October restricts Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to the bank's engineers, Bloomberg News reported, following a review of productivity and risk concerns.Strats, who work across trading, quantitative research and software engineering, still have access, according to a second person familiar with the matter.The change has frustrated some traders, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. They had been using the tools to monitor client trading flows, model market moves and positions, and put together written and graphic material. Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra said the bank makes certain AI tools available to staff "to determine the best use cases" across the firm.Argenti was praising trader-built tools in JulyAs recently as July, chief information officer Marco Argenti was talking up "vibe coding" by Goldman's non-technical employees. He told Bloomberg that traders and bankers had built tools with AI and passed them to the firm's engineers, of whom there are about 12,000, to be improved.That arrangement let the people closest to a problem build a first version without waiting for engineering time. It also meant thousands of employees without engineering training were running software that writes and executes code, on the same machines they use to handle client information.At a conference in Turin last month, Argenti described Goldman's AI adoption in waves and said developers, more than 12,000 of the bank's roughly 47,000 staff, had made up the first. The October guidance limits the coding agents to that group.Goldman restricted Claude in Hong Kong in AprilIn April, Goldman removed Claude from its internal AI platform for bankers in Hong Kong. The Financial Times reported that the bank had read its contract with Anthropic strictly, and an Anthropic spokesperson said Claude had never been officially supported in Hong Kong. ChatGPT and Gemini remained available there. JPMorgan removed Claude from its Hong Kong approved list in June.The Hong Kong restriction was based on location and contract terms, and the new one is based on role. Goldman's in-house AI assistant, which uses models from several companies, is still available across the firm. The restriction applies to third-party agents that can write and run code by themselves.Goldman is still working closely with AnthropicEarlier this year, Goldman said Anthropic engineers had spent six months at the bank helping build Claude-based agents for trade accounting and client onboarding. Those agents sit in the back office and are run by Goldman's engineering teams.Goldman and Morgan Stanley are also the lead underwriters on Anthropic's IPO, according to the S-1 filed October 26. Anthropic is expected to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT before the end of November, as we reported last week. Over the next few weeks, Goldman's bankers will be marketing shares in a company whose coding agent most of them are no longer allowed to use.Why a coding agent is riskier on a trading deskClaude Code reads files, writes programs and runs them, typically with the same access as the person using it. Code an engineer writes with it usually goes through review, testing and deployment controls before it reaches anything important. A script a trader builds to watch client flows can end up in daily use without going through any of those.Banks are also required to keep information barriers between groups, for example between bankers working on deals and traders who could profit from knowing about them. Goldman built its internal AI platform around controls like these. A tool a trader puts together with an agent wasn't designed with them in mind, and engineers can only check it if someone sends it their way.There is also the matter of whether anyone understands the code. Last month a Meta engineer said he now ships code he can't fully account for, and writing software is his job. A trader using an agent to model positions is less likely to know how that code handles unusual cases, which on a trading desk can mean losses.Cost may also have played a part. Agent usage is billed by the token, and several companies that gave agents to everyone have seen spending climb. Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard after employees ran agents on pointless tasks to move up it, and Accenture now funds $29 a month of Claude per employee. Bloomberg's sources said productivity was part of Goldman's review.Barclays is moving in the other directionBarclays said in October that it expects half its developers to be using Claude Code by the end of the year, and three weeks later named developers among 5,000 job cuts. Like Goldman, it is giving coding agents to engineers. Unlike Goldman, it is also using them to reduce how many engineers it employs.Banks have tightened agent access in other places this fall. JPMorgan and Schwab are blocking outside agents from customer accounts, and Goldman has now set limits on which of its own employees can use them.Our takeAt State of AI, we think Goldman was right to restrict the tools and wrong in how it went about it.A trading floor is a bad place for unreviewed code written by people who can't read it, and the information barrier problem would be reason enough on its own. Requiring that agent-written code come from people trained to review it is a sensible rule for a regulated business.Goldman's own CIO was promoting traders' AI-built tools in July, though. Withdrawing access through a guideline update, with no replacement mentioned in Bloomberg's reporting, tells the traders who found good uses that they were the risk. Their complaints point to work the engineering team could take on, and Goldman would get more out of collecting them than out of waiting for them to fade.Leaders at other companies should settle who owns agent-built code before handing agents out. When someone outside engineering builds a tool with Claude Code or Copilot, a named engineer should take responsibility for it before it touches production data.Existing controls should cover code an agent writes. Information barriers, data entitlements and software approval rules still apply when the code came from a prompt.And when a tool is taken away, it's worth recording what people were using it for. Goldman's traders were watching client flows and modeling positions, and they will still need to do both.

comments.author: bcherny
comments.textZhHtml:
Boris from the Claude Code team here. Historically Claude Code has not done secret scrubbing (there are many good tools for that), but we are looking into what we can do to prevent this.

That said, a few thoughts:

1. .claude/settings.local.json is meant to stay local. This is not a file you should check into source control. We automatically gitignore it when Claude creates the file, so in this case the files were manually created and checked in (docs: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings)

2. Permission rules are old hat. Everyone should be using auto mode instead. It is safer and also does not require manually maintaining finicky allow/deny lists. Auto mode is enabled by default and is included for free in all plans.

3. Regardless of what agent you use, you should have secret scanning enabled. GitHub and other source control hosts offer it. There are many threat models that it protects against and you should absolutely use it if you can. (see https://github.com/security/plans)

I've been ripped (on this site) for making this prediction. While the frontier (i.e. The toughest problems) will always push the limits of available computing power, what typical people do with AI won't always be on the frontier, nor will what appears on the frontier necessarily be lucrative. The frontier used to be playing Chess, Atari, and Go. These were challenging and really advanced AI, but they didn't make a lot of money. Now a phone can do these things.

You're an example of this process. You used to require a frontier model running on a data centre. Algorithms improved and, perhaps, your hardware as well, but your requirements didn't go up. Now you can do what you need to do with local hardware. You're one AI user who might not need to send money to Anthropic going forward unless you find a new frontier application that interests you.

This is why I'm a little bearish when it comes to the valuation of the AI giants. Yes, there are some extremely lucrative things on the frontier right now but, in the future, people may shift a lot of what they're doing now to local hardware while new things on the frontier may not produce the kind of profits that will pay back trillions in debt. AI companies have bet big on themselves being able to constantly and perpetually find new applications, and also that those new applications will make money.
